Name: threshold_behavioral_response_seir
Title: Modeling Threshold-Based Behavioral Responses in SEIR Dynamics
Experiment: Modify the seir_eq function to implement multiple thresholds for adjusting the contact rate based on the proportion of infected individuals. Define specific behavior change scenarios (e.g., reduced contact rates at 1%, 5%, 10% infection levels) and analyze their impacts on peak infections and total infections. This will allow for a more detailed understanding of how varying public health responses can influence disease spread.

Name: budget_constrained_intervention_timing
Title: Optimizing the Timing of Finite Intervention Budgets in SEIR Epidemics
Experiment: Modify the SEIR integration so that beta is time-dependent: beta_t = beta0 * (1 - u[t]), where u[t] is a bounded contact-reduction schedule. Implement several schedules with equal cumulative intervention effort, including early intervention, late intervention, continuous low-intensity intervention, single pulses, and split pulses. Perform a coarse grid search over intervention start times, durations, and intensities under a fixed budget constraint. For each schedule, integrate the model using the corresponding beta_t and record infected_peak, infected_peak_day, and total_infected. Compare schedules that optimize peak infections against schedules that optimize final epidemic size, and generate a Pareto frontier of peak versus cumulative infections. Repeat the comparison over grids of beta, latent period, infectious period, and initial infectious population to assess robustness. Store baseline and schedule-specific trajectories and summary metrics in final_info.json for visualization.

Name: early_data_identifiability_seir
Title: How Much Can Early Epidemic Data Identify? Equifinal SEIR Models and Forecast Uncertainty
Experiment: Generate a synthetic ground-truth SEIR trajectory using the existing model, then expose only the first W days of infectious observations, with configurable Gaussian or Poisson-like noise and a fixed random seed. Implement a parameter-grid calibration over beta, latent period lp, infectious period ip, and optionally the initial infectious count. For each candidate parameter set, integrate the model with odeint and calculate a loss against the observed early trajectory, using either infectious counts alone or infectious plus recovered counts. Retain all candidate models whose loss is within a chosen tolerance of the best fit, rather than only selecting one optimum. Simulate these near-equivalent models over the complete 100-day horizon and record infected_peak_day, infected_peak, total_infected, parameter values, and early-data loss. Repeat for several observation-window lengths, noise levels, and observation modalities. Save the ground truth, observations, calibrated parameter ensemble, trajectories, uncertainty intervals, and summary metrics in final_info.json. Analyze whether excellent early fits can yield substantially different later epidemic forecasts, which parameters are correlated or poorly identified, and how much longer observation or additional compartment data reduces forecast uncertainty.

Name: stochastic_extinction_seir
Title: When Deterministic SEIR Forecasts Fail: Stochastic Extinction and Epidemic Risk
Experiment: Add a continuous-time stochastic SEIR simulator using the Gillespie algorithm. Represent the state as integer counts [S, E, I, R], with event rates beta*S*I for new infections, E/lp for latent-to-infectious transitions, and I/ip for recoveries. Simulate many independent realizations up to the existing 100-day horizon, recording trajectories at integer days and computing infected_peak, infected_peak_day, final recovered count, and whether the outbreak becomes extinct or reaches a specified major-outbreak threshold. Compare stochastic means, medians, prediction intervals, extinction probabilities, and conditional major-outbreak statistics with the deterministic odeint trajectory. Sweep over beta, initial infectious count, total population size, latent period, and infectious period; include parameter settings below, near, and above the deterministic threshold. For each setting, store aggregate distributions, representative trajectories, quantile bands, and the deterministic baseline in final_info.json rather than saving every realization. Include a convergence experiment that increases the number of stochastic replicates and a population-scaling experiment to test when stochastic results approach the deterministic model. The main analyses should quantify how often the deterministic trajectory is atypical, how strongly early extinction changes expected final epidemic size, and how uncertainty is concentrated near the invasion threshold.

Name: optimal_surveillance_design_seir
Title: Designing Sparse Surveillance Strategies for Reliable SEIR Forecasts
Experiment: Extend the experiment with a synthetic-observation and experimental-design framework. First generate a ground-truth SEIR trajectory using the existing model. Construct a candidate parameter library over beta, latent period lp, infectious period ip, and optionally initial infectious count. For every candidate, integrate the trajectory over the full horizon and derive possible observables including infectious prevalence I(t), incidence beta*S(t)*I(t), and cumulative recovered count R(t). Add configurable Gaussian or Poisson-like observation noise with a fixed seed. Define a fixed surveillance budget B, where each observation consists of selecting one observable type and one time point. Compare predefined schedules such as uniform sampling, early-only sampling, late-only sampling, random sampling, prevalence-only sampling, and mixed-compartment sampling. Also implement sequential greedy schedules: after each observation, reweight candidate models according to their observation likelihood and select the next time/observable that maximizes expected reduction in posterior entropy or predictive variance for infected_peak, infected_peak_day, and total_infected. Evaluate schedules across multiple ground-truth parameter settings, noise levels, budgets, and misspecified initial conditions. For each schedule, record posterior parameter distributions, forecast intervals, entropy reduction, predictive interval width, forecast bias, and the regret of selecting the wrong epidemic-risk category. Store representative trajectories, observation schedules, and aggregate value-of-information curves in final_info.json. Include ablations comparing adaptive versus non-adaptive schedules and prevalence observations versus incidence or recovery observations. The main analysis should identify when sparse targeted measurements outperform frequent uniform monitoring, quantify the marginal value of each additional observation, and test whether the best schedule for parameter identification is also the best schedule for forecasting epidemic outcomes.

Name: seir_structural_misspecification_stress_test
Title: When a Good SEIR Fit Predicts Poorly: Stress-Testing Epidemic Forecasts Under Structural Misspecification
Experiment: Implement several synthetic truth-model extensions that generate epidemic trajectories but are not available to the forecasting model: (1) smoothly time-varying transmission beta(t), (2) abrupt transmission changepoints, (3) waning immunity through an SIRS-like extension, and (4) low-rate imported infections. Preserve the original constant-parameter SEIR model as the misspecified forecasting model. For each truth model and parameter setting, generate noisy observations of infectious prevalence, incidence, or recovered counts over an early observation window. Fit the constant SEIR model using a grid over beta, latent period, infectious period, and optionally initial infectious count, selecting either the best fit or all near-equivalent fits. Forecast the unobserved remainder of the horizon and compare early-window loss with errors in infected_peak, infected_peak_day, total_infected, and trajectory-wide prediction intervals. Add rolling re-estimation experiments in which the constant SEIR parameters are refit as new observations arrive, and compare these against one-time early calibration. Evaluate whether additional observables, longer training windows, residual-based change detection, or uncertainty ensembles can identify structural failure. Store truth trajectories, observations, fitted parameters, forecast trajectories, residual diagnostics, metric errors, and calibration-versus-forecast plots in final_info.json. Report cases where the misspecified model achieves an excellent early fit but makes large long-term errors, and quantify which observation types and adaptation strategies most reduce this failure.

Name: delay_robust_feedback_control_seir
Title: Delayed Feedback Control in Epidemics: Stability, Oscillations, and Robust Intervention Design
Experiment: Replace the single odeint call with a day-by-day SEIR integrator that permits beta to change according to a feedback controller. Implement several policies: instantaneous proportional control based on current infectious prevalence, delayed proportional control based on I from d days earlier, smoothed control based on a moving average, single-threshold control, and hysteresis control with separate activation and relaxation thresholds. Add configurable reporting noise, reporting delay, implementation delay, maximum intervention strength, and maximum daily change in intervention intensity. At each day, use only information available up to that day to select beta for the next integration interval. Compare controllers over grids of delay, control gain, hysteresis width, latent period, infectious period, baseline beta, and initial infections. Record infected_peak, infected_peak_day, total_infected, cumulative intervention intensity, number of intervention switches, total time under restrictions, number and magnitude of rebound peaks, and trajectory smoothness. Construct phase diagrams showing regions of stable suppression, delayed overshoot, persistent oscillation, and ineffective control. Include ablations for perfect versus noisy observations, no implementation lag versus realistic lag, and proportional versus hysteretic control. Store representative trajectories, controller histories, parameter settings, and aggregate performance summaries in final_info.json. The main analysis should test whether delay measured relative to the infectious period predicts instability, whether hysteresis reduces policy chattering and rebound waves, and which controller achieves the best infection-control versus intervention-burden tradeoff under parameter misspecification.

Name: hidden_heterogeneity_aggregation_seir
Title: When Can a Population-Averaged SEIR Model Be Trusted? Epidemic Forecasting Under Hidden Heterogeneity
Experiment: Extend the single-population SEIR model to a multi-group SEIR system with G groups. For each group g, maintain S_g, E_g, I_g, and R_g and define force of infection lambda_g = beta * susceptibility_g * sum_h(C_gh * infectiousness_h * I_h / N_h), where C is a configurable contact matrix. Implement homogeneous mixing, assortative mixing, disassortative mixing, and random contact matrices. Generate heterogeneous populations with controlled variation in susceptibility, infectiousness, group size, and contact activity. Also retain the original one-group model as a baseline. For every heterogeneous setting, construct a matched homogeneous model by calibrating its beta so that it has the same initial aggregate exponential growth rate or the same dominant next-generation-matrix eigenvalue. Initialize models with the same aggregate infectious prevalence and compare aggregate trajectories over 100 days. Record infected_peak, infected_peak_day, total_infected, aggregate incidence, group-specific attack rates, time-varying effective reproduction numbers, and the error made by the homogeneous approximation. Sweep the coefficient of variation of susceptibility and contact activity, the number of groups, mixing assortativity, latent period, infectious period, baseline transmission, and initial infections. Include an intervention ablation in which equal total contact-reduction effort is applied uniformly across groups versus preferentially to high-activity or high-susceptibility groups, while keeping the no-intervention heterogeneous and homogeneous baselines separate. Analyze whether matching early growth is sufficient to predict final epidemic size, identify regimes where heterogeneity causes overestimation or underestimation of peak and final infections, and produce phase diagrams of homogeneous-model forecast error as a function of heterogeneity and mixing structure. Store representative group trajectories, aggregate trajectories, matched parameters, contact matrices, summary metrics, and parameter-sweep results in final_info.json.

Name: dimensionless_seir_scaling
Title: Universal Scaling Laws and Dimensionless Regimes in SEIR Epidemics
Experiment: Extend the experiment with a systematic scaling and nondimensionalization study. Implement a normalized SEIR solver using population fractions s=S/N, e=E/N, i=I/N, and r=R/N, and define dimensionless time tau=t/ip. For each parameter setting, compute the effective dimensionless groups R0=beta*N*ip, rho=lp/ip, and the initial fractions e0, i0. Generate many parameter combinations spanning population sizes, beta values, latent periods, infectious periods, and initial conditions. Construct matched ensembles in which raw parameters differ substantially but R0, rho, and initial fractions are held fixed. Compare trajectories in normalized time and population units, measuring collapse error for S, E, I, and R. Separately evaluate how infected_peak/N, peak timing/ip, final recovered fraction, early growth rate, and epidemic duration vary as functions of R0, rho, and initialization. Create response surfaces over R0 and rho, including subcritical, near-threshold, and strongly supercritical regimes. Test whether final epidemic size is approximately invariant at fixed R0, whether peak prevalence requires the additional latent-period ratio, and whether peak timing follows a transferable scaling relation with ip. Include perturbation experiments in which one dimensionless group is changed while the others remain fixed, plus numerical checks using different time steps and integration horizons. Store representative raw and normalized trajectories, matched parameter sets, collapse errors, dimensionless response surfaces, and summary metrics in final_info.json. The main analysis should identify universal quantities, quantify finite-initial-condition effects, and provide a scale-free regime map that can transfer conclusions across population sizes and time units.

Name: seir_frequency_response
Title: Resonance, Phase Lag, and Memory in Periodically Forced SEIR Epidemics
Experiment: Extend the model with a time-dependent transmission rate and an optional importation term. Implement a day-by-day integrator for dS, dE, dI, and dR, using beta(t) = beta0 * (1 + a_beta * sin(2*pi*t/T + phi)) for seasonal or behavioral forcing, and optionally add periodic infections through dE += m(t), where m(t) = m0 * (1 + a_m * sin(2*pi*t/T + phi_m)). Preserve the original constant-beta trajectory as an unforced baseline. Sweep forcing periods T across values shorter than, comparable to, and longer than the latent and infectious periods; vary forcing amplitude, phase, baseline beta, latent period, infectious period, initial infectious population, and population size. Include subcritical, near-threshold, and supercritical regimes. For each setting, simulate enough cycles to distinguish transients from the long-run response, and repeat with several forcing phases. Estimate the amplitude and phase lag of infectious prevalence and incidence using sinusoidal regression or Fourier coefficients, along with transient amplification, cumulative infections, peak prevalence, number of epidemic waves, and harmonic distortion. Run small-amplitude experiments to estimate a local linear frequency-response curve, then compare them with larger-amplitude nonlinear responses. Add ablations comparing transmission forcing, importation forcing, combined forcing, and a constant-input baseline with equal mean transmission or equal mean importations. Store forcing parameters, representative trajectories, baseline trajectories, response amplitudes, phase lags, harmonic ratios, epidemic metrics, and parameter-sweep summaries in final_info.json. Produce a regime map identifying attenuation, resonance-like amplification, phase reversal, and nonlinear multi-wave behavior. The main analysis should determine whether the dominant response timescale is set by the latent period, infectious period, or their interaction; quantify when periodic environmental variation materially changes epidemic risk despite unchanged mean beta; and assess whether prevalence or incidence provides a more informative signal of the underlying forcing frequency.

Name: critical_slowing_down_seir
Title: Detecting Epidemic Invasion Thresholds Through Critical Slowing Down in SEIR Dynamics
Experiment: Extend the experiment with a local-stability and perturbation-response framework around the disease-free equilibrium. First derive or numerically estimate the SEIR Jacobian near [S,E,I,R]=[N,0,0,0], where N is the total population, and sweep beta across values below, near, and above the invasion threshold beta*N*ip=1. For each beta, latent period lp, infectious period ip, population size, and small initial introduction, integrate the model for a sufficiently long horizon using a finer time grid than the current one-day grid. Estimate early exponential growth or decay rates from log(I(t)+epsilon), the dominant Jacobian eigenvalue, time to return after a perturbation, integrated perturbation amplification, epidemic onset delay, and eventual peak and final size. Add transient pulse experiments that temporarily increase E or I at selected times, then measure the resulting deviation from an unperturbed trajectory and its decay time. Compare perturbations to the exposed compartment, infectious compartment, and both compartments, and vary perturbation magnitude to separate linear from nonlinear responses. Include optional synthetic measurement noise and sparse observation schedules to test whether empirical indicators such as lag-1 autocorrelation, variance, recovery time, and trend estimates can identify proximity to the threshold. Normalize results by population size and infectious period, and compare predictions from the linearized system with the nonlinear odeint trajectories. Store threshold parameters, Jacobian eigenvalues, perturbation-response curves, early-warning statistics, representative trajectories, and parameter-sweep summaries in final_info.json. The main analysis should identify which indicators are most reliable before a large outbreak occurs, quantify how latent periods modify critical slowing down, determine the observation horizon required to distinguish near-critical from clearly subcritical dynamics, and characterize where finite introductions or nonlinear depletion invalidate local stability predictions.
